title: Yajnavalkya and his two wives: he's leaving (2.4)
hook: the greatest sage in the book tells his wife he's leaving home for good, and offers to split the property
tomorrow: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, priya: the self is dearer than a son, because it is more inward. Your line was love the self.

A kitchen, a long marriage, an ordinary evening. And the husband says: I'm going. Not to another house. Not to another person. He's leaving the householder's life altogether, to wander with nothing. Before I go, he says, let me divide what I have between you and my other wife, so it's settled. So begins one of the Brihadaranyaka's great conversations. The man is Yajnavalkya, and today is about what it meant, in his world, to leave.
screen: `I'M GOING.` → `NOT TO ANOTHER HOUSE.` → `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is a leading voice of this Upanishad. Tradition credits him with a whole branch of the Veda, the White Yajurveda, and in a few days you'll watch him take on a room full of rivals. Here he's at home, with two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani. That's nearly all this chapter tells us about them. When the scene is told again later in the book, it adds one line: Maitreyi was one who discussed Brahman, and Katyayani had, in the text's short phrase, a woman's knowledge, words readers interpret in different ways. The text never tells us what Katyayani thought, or how either of them felt, and it's fair to say so. Why is he leaving? Hindu tradition later described life in four stages: the student, the householder, the forest dweller, and the renunciant, the sannyasi, who gives up home, property and name, and wanders. Yajnavalkya is stepping from the second stage toward the last. In the retelling, the verb is the one used for going forth into that wandering life. And notice what he does first. He doesn't vanish in the night. He sits down and tries to settle the property fairly. Even leaving everything, he wants to leave well. This whole conversation appears twice in the Brihadaranyaka, in book two and again in book four, with small differences, and the book keeps both tellings. What keeps the scene alive is what Maitreyi says next.
screen: `A LEADING VOICE OF THIS UPANISHAD.` · `TWO WIVES; THE TEXT SAYS LITTLE MORE.` · `FROM HOUSEHOLDER TO WANDERER.` · `TOLD TWICE IN THE SAME BOOK.` · then, large: `THE MAN WHO LEFT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're getting ready to leave, or will one day: a job, a house, a role, a habit, a stage of life. Don't decide anything; just ask what Yajnavalkya asked: what would it take to settle this fairly, so the people around it are cared for? Let one small answer come, then let the question go and rest with the breath.
Sannyasa, renunciation, laying everything down. He is leaving home for good, and first offers to settle his property between Maitreyi and Katyayani.
Your line: the man who left. Tomorrow, Maitreyi answers him with a question. See you then.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition sannyasa is taken by formal vows, often late in life, after which the renunciant leaves home and property behind; the four stages of life are an ideal pattern described in the dharma texts, and the householder's life is honored in its own right.

original.note: Sanskrit saṃnyāsa: laying everything down. the fourth and last stage of life in the dharma texts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man walking out on his family.
what it means: Yajnavalkya is going forth as a wandering renunciant, and settles his property first.
what a scholar hears: the scene is told twice (2.4 and 4.5). only the second telling describes the wives, and uses the verb for going forth into the wandering life.

chat.says: Wait, Yajnavalkya just walks out on his wives? What's going on in that story?
options: He's going forth as a wanderer, and first he sits down to settle his property fairly.
He's angry at Katyayani and leaves to marry a third wife in another village.
He's sent away by the king for losing a debate, so he hands over his things.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya is leaving the householder's life for the wanderer's, and first offers to divide what he has between Maitreyi and Katyayani.

notes: 4.5.1 describes Maitreyi as brahmavādinī and Katyayani as strīprajñā; rendered gently as 'the knowledge most women of her day had'. A Keeper may prefer different wording.
2.4.1 uses udyāsyan (going up/away from this state); 4.5.2 uses pravrajiṣyan (about to go forth as a renunciant). Confirm.
Tradition credits Yajnavalkya with the White (Shukla) Yajurveda; confirm phrasing.
The four ashramas are a later dharma-text scheme; the script says 'Hindu tradition later described'. Confirm.
